title: BERT: Pretraining Deep Bidirectional Transformers
hook: What if a model read a sentence both directions at once? BERT did, by masking words and predicting them — and made pretrain-then-fine-tune the default recipe in NLP.
key_points: Pretrains a Transformer encoder by masking ~15% of tokens and predicting them from surrounding context.
Reads context bidirectionally, so each word sees both its left and right neighbors.
One pretrained model fine-tunes to many tasks: classification, tagging, question answering.
Encoder-only design makes it strong at understanding text, not generating it.
Popularized the pretrain-then-fine-tune workflow across NLP.
content_html: BERT, from Devlin and colleagues at Google in 2018, pretrains a Transformer encoder by hiding random words and asking the model to fill them back in. Because it can use words on both sides of the gap, it builds rich, context-aware representations. You then fine-tune that one model on your specific task, and it set new bars across a broad NLP benchmark suite.
extra_html:
How it works

BERT corrupts the input by masking about 15% of the tokens, then trains the encoder to predict the hidden words from everything around them — left and right context at the same time. This "masked language modeling" objective forces the model to learn how words relate. After pretraining on large text corpora, you bolt a small task-specific head on top and fine-tune the whole thing on labeled data.

Why it matters

BERT showed you can learn language understanding once, from raw text, then cheaply adapt it to many downstream tasks instead of training each from scratch. That pretrain-then-fine-tune pattern became the backbone of modern NLP. Its encoder-only, bidirectional design remains the go-to for understanding tasks like search ranking, classification, and entity extraction, where you analyze text rather than generate it.

flashcards.back_html: It is an encoder trained with masked language modeling — it predicts hidden words from everything around them, so each token sees neighbors on both sides at once.

flashcards.prompt: Why is BERT's encoder-only design better suited to understanding than to generation?

choices.text: It's built to analyze text bidirectionally, not to produce text left-to-right
It has too few parameters to generate fluent text
It was never trained on natural language

flashcards.explanation_html: The encoder reads context both directions to build representations, making it strong for tasks like classification and QA rather than text generation.

flashcards.prompt: What workflow did BERT popularize across NLP?
